lead.headline: Hacker leaves players alone at the logon prompt
lead.dek: Activision turns a simulated computer connection into a mystery without a rule book.
body: A computer connection appears to be going wrong. Activision president Jim Levy struggles to reach headquarters, then reveals that the apparent remote session is the game itself. October’s COMPUTE! recounts the demonstration in its fall-games survey: Hacker makes uncertainty its opening attraction, rather than a problem to be explained away in a manual.

There are no instructions, rules or clues to consult. Players must discover whose simulated computer they have reached, what they are trying to accomplish and what will end their attempt. This is a fictional telecomputing puzzle played on a home computer, not access to a real remote service. The screen’s invitation is theatrical, and the investigation belongs to the game.

The magazine lists initial Commodore 64/128 versions, with Apple and Atari editions to follow, and gives the price as not yet announced. Those are the survey’s plans; they do not establish that every version has reached shops during this week. The demonstration itself is not dated in the report.

Hacker shares the fall desk with MicroProse’s submarine simulation Silent Service, Datasoft’s Alternate Reality: The City and Sierra’s King’s Quest II. The competition is widening from reflexes to discovery, command and worlds that reward patient exploration. For the Commodore player, a blinking prompt may now be as enticing as a screen full of targets.

stories.headline: Atari’s $799 desktop puts a mouse and 512K within reach
body: Atari’s 520ST is becoming widely available, according to Tom R. Halfhill’s October COMPUTE! hands-on report. Its 512K of memory and 8-MHz Motorola 68000 serve a mouse-driven GEM desktop with icons, windows and drop-down menus. The machine was announced in January; this is the autumn buying desk, not a new launch announcement.

The report’s $799 monochrome package includes the computer, external floppy drive, monitor, mouse and system software. A color-monitor package is quoted at $999. Monochrome gives 640 by 400 pixels at 70 Hz; color offers either four colors at 640 by 200 or sixteen at 320 by 200 from a 512-color palette.

Built-in MIDI, RS-232 and Centronics connections give musicians, modem users and printer owners room to work. Logo accompanies the system, while BASIC was still unfinished when the reporter wrote. Buyers should distinguish what is in that package from future storage products and prototypes.

stories.headline: Amiga promises PC software without an 8088 board
body: The new Amiga faces a familiar question: what can it run? October’s COMPUTE! revisits Commodore’s July 23 Lincoln Center demonstration, where an engineer loaded a software PC emulator, booted PC-DOS 2.10 through an optional external 5¼-inch drive and demonstrated Lotus 1-2-3. No 8088 expansion board was part of the demonstration.

Commodore claimed the emulator occupied about 40K of RAM excluding video memory, but the report records doubts about matching a real PC’s speed. A successful demonstration is not a promise that every PC program will work well. No emulator price was announced, and the company’s availability forecast is not proof of delivery.

The quoted base Amiga costs $1,295 with 256K of user RAM. Another 256K of writable control store holds the disk-loaded system image; it is not extra general-purpose user memory. The report lists a $200 option to reach 512K user RAM, alongside announced software including Graphicraft, Textcraft, Telecraft, ABasiC and Lattice C.

stories.headline: 2400-bit modems become an affordable step up
body: The price of a faster bulletin-board evening is coming down. October’s COMPUTE! reports a $695 list price for U.S. Robotics’ Courier 2400, against $895 for Hayes and $795 for most competitors. These are modem prices, not the online-service bill.

The Courier puts command and register references underneath its case, offers three callable help screens and keeps DIP switches and speaker volume within reach. U.S. Robotics is also working with operators of busy bulletin boards on an acquisition program intended to encourage 2400-bps access; the column names no particular board or sysop.

The Source added 2400-bps access in August. October’s quoted premiums are $1.80 per prime-time hour and $1.20 per nonprime hour above its 1200-bps prices of $25.80 and $10.80. For a less expensive hardware entry, Cermetek’s internal Infomate 1200-TPC is listed at $198, but it is a 1200-bps modem rather than a 2400-bps substitute.

editorNote: A logon mystery leads the fall games desk; mouse-driven desktops and cheaper modems fill the workbench.

market.headline: Speed costs more than the modem
market.summary: The Source’s quoted nonprime 1200-bps service is $10.80 an hour; its 2400-bps premium adds $1.20. Prime-time figures are $25.80 plus $1.80. Hardware and connection charges belong in the same budget.

worldAnchor.headline: Challenger launches German Spacelab D-1
worldAnchor.summary: Challenger launched October 30 at noon EST with an eight-person crew and the German Spacelab D-1 mission. The laboratory carries 75 numbered experiments, with some operations controlled from Oberpfaffenhofen near Munich.

curiosity.headline: The new Atari terminal skips one increasingly popular speed
curiosity.summary: A reporter found 300, 1200, 4800 and 9600 bps in an ST terminal accessory’s menu—but no 2400.
curiosity.detail: October COMPUTE!’s telecomputing columnist describes a visit to Atari and a demonstrator changing the subject to a graphics demo after the missing speed was pointed out. Treat it as an observed software version, not proof that ST hardware cannot communicate at 2400 bps.

gadgetWatch.headline: A cellular modem carries a four-figure forecast
gadgetWatch.summary: October COMPUTE! reports AT&T Technologies and Bell Atlantic trials in the Baltimore–Washington area since July of a 2400-bps CTS-1620 cellular modem, expected in 1986 at $1,600–$2,600. It requires a cellular telephone/transmitter and an input/display device. Already available lower-speed alternatives are reported as Motorola 300 bps at $195 and Spectrum Cellular 1200 bps at $695. Trials and forecasts are not this week’s product releases.
